initial_requirements: European card-issuing authorities need a shared TACHOnet service to coordinate driver smart-card requests across participating member organizations. Users should be able to ask one or more members about the possible delivery or status of cards, receive standardized replies, and follow each request through completion. The service should also manage access rights, alert participants when expected replies are late, and provide operational statistics.

slots.key: Delivery failure notification and retry/escalation handling
slots.value: A delivery failure should notify the originating authority first. The responding authority is additionally informed when the failure concerns their reply or when they need to resend. If a national setup includes a supervising or administering role, that role can also be copied in for persistent failures, repeated timeouts, or cases needing operational intervention. Notification scope depends on the authority’s configured responsibility model and agreed escalation rules for the network. Retries may be allowed only for technical transport failures and only on channels where the sender controls delivery, while they should be suppressed for business rejections or messages that have already been definitively answered. Some message types may be too time-sensitive to retry many times, so they would escalate sooner, and in some setups the responding authority may own the retry action rather than the originating authority. Business-level rejections, validation errors, unauthorized requests, and malformed messages should go straight to review or escalation rather than being retried automatically.

If the failure is clearly permanent, such as an invalid address or unauthorized recipient, repeated retries should be suppressed and the issue logged as a non-recoverable delivery problem.

slots.key: Delivery failure notification and retry policy
slots.value: On delivery failure, notify the originating authority; if the failure is on a reply path, also notify the responding authority. Repeat only for temporary technical transport failures and only on channels where the sender controls delivery. Some time-sensitive message types may go to escalation sooner with fewer retries, and in some setups the responding authority may own the retry action rather than the originating authority. topics.topic_content: Service continuity for participating authorities

slots.value: Available continuously in principle; planned maintenance windows are allowed and should be scheduled outside normal business peaks where possible, with advance notice to participants. Standard maintenance should get at least 48 hours' notice; longer or more disruptive work should get several business days' notice. Urgent security or incident-driven maintenance may have shorter notice, but it should still be communicated as soon as possible to all participants. Emergency work remains an exception rather than the norm. The outage window should be bounded and published in advance. Maintenance-related outages are confirmed once the planned maintenance starts at the published time, or earlier if the service owner sends an explicit notice that the outage has begun or is unavoidable; if the maintenance is only a warning or possible delay, the contingency should not be triggered yet. A partial outage should trigger contingency earlier if it affects message flow or response handling enough to make the service unreliable. For phased shutdowns, the hold-or-contingency process starts when the participant-dependent function is actually taken out of service, not when preparatory work begins. If a maintenance notice is withdrawn, contingency should not start, or should be ended immediately if it was announced in error.

slots.value: Everything has to stay traceable for operational follow-up and audit, with each step recorded in enough detail to reconstruct the exchange later: who initiated it, which authority it was sent to, when it was sent, what status it had, and what the reply or refusal was. Status changes should be timestamped and linked to the same request so the full history is visible. The record should also show whether the response was on time, whether reminders or alerts were issued, and whether the case was closed normally or escalated. Nothing important should be left as an untraceable free-text note. At submission, this includes a unique request identifier, the sending authority, the receiving authority, the card or driver reference being queried, the request type or purpose, the submission timestamp, the current status, and any priority flags, due dates, or correlation details from a previous exchange. For parallel inquiries, each request must still tie back to one master request ID, with each recipient having its own linked sub-reference or message instance so replies, refusals, reminders, and non-responses remain visible in the same case history and can be attributed to the correct authority. At the escalation point, record the deadline used, the timestamp when it became overdue, what reminder or escalation was triggered, who it was sent to, the current request state, the recipient authority, and any prior follow-up attempts. The exact list of escalation and reminder event types is left undecided for now, but the audit trail must capture that reminders, overdue notices, and escalations happened, with each such event timestamped, tied to the right request, and traceable back to the receiving authority. Repeated reminders should each be logged as separate events, multiple recipient authorities should each keep their own linked event history under the master request, and if an escalation follows a partial reply, that partial reply must remain visible so the reason for escalation is clear. Nothing should overwrite or hide earlier actions, and each event must link back both to the original request and to the specific recipient or response it relates to. If a reply is incomplete or ambiguous, the original response should be preserved in the audit trail exactly as received. Once it’s closed, it should move to a completed or closed state and stop generating normal workflow reminders. A final audit entry and completion notification to the requesting party should occur, and reopening is generally treated as a new request unless the operations team decides the old case should be corrected due to a clear mistake or incomplete processing. If the reply is only slightly unclear, a human operator can resolve it locally when the missing or unclear part can be resolved from information already in the request or from our own records without making assumptions; if the operator would have to guess, or if the answer affects the legal or operational meaning of the request, it must go back for clarification. Small formatting issues or minor wording ambiguities may be corrected or interpreted locally when the intent is still obvious, and that decision must be recorded in the audit trail.

slots.key: Record retention period by participating authority
slots.value: Each participating authority should configure its own retention period within the shared framework, using the longest mandatory period that applies to that authority for the record type in question, unless a national rule explicitly requires earlier deletion. Privacy and public-records obligations can differ by country, and the exact limit for operational traceability and audit must still be verified with the legal and records teams; at minimum, request metadata and status history should be kept for the required period. If there is an active legal hold, dispute, or audit requirement, the record should be kept until that hold is released, regardless of the normal retention end. If there is no hold, the default should be deletion or anonymization depending on what the national rule allows for that record type.

slots.value: Queued requests should remain stored until the service is restored, rather than being rerouted automatically, because automatic rerouting could break coordination and the audit trail. The fallback mode should apply only when the central TACHOnet service or its core messaging path is confirmed unavailable. Participating authorities should be told to hold new traffic or follow a predefined manual contingency process. If a separately approved alternate path exists, it must be explicitly configured and governed; automatic rerouting is not the default. For maintenance-related outages, treat the outage as confirmed once planned maintenance starts at the published time, or earlier if the service owner sends an explicit notice that the outage has begun or is unavoidable; participating authorities should switch to the hold-or-contingency process immediately and should not wait for a failed request. If maintenance is only a warning or a possible delay, do not trigger the contingency yet. A partial outage should trigger the hold-or-contingency process earlier if it affects message flow or response handling in a way that makes the service unreliable. For a phased shutdown, start the process when the affected function participants depend on is actually taken out of service, not when preparatory work starts. If a maintenance notice is withdrawn, the contingency should not start, or should be ended immediately if it had already been announced in error.

slots.value: If the reason for the inquiry or the authority’s role changes who can see the request, who should answer it, or how quickly it must be handled, it must be recorded as structured metadata and used by the workflow; if it is only descriptive and does not change processing, it can be kept as reference information.
